A toilet seat is all that stands between Dima Awad and moving out of her makeshift tent before winter.
The 48-year-old Palestinian mother has rented a small garage in western Gaza City and has already moved most of her belongings there.
But she cannot move in until she finds a toilet seat, something that has become increasingly difficult to find in Gaza.
The basic item is among a range of essential goods that Israel continues to prevent from entering the besieged enclave.
“I paid the rent around 10 days ago, and I’ve been looking for a proper toilet at an affordable price for about two weeks now,” said Awad, who now lives with her only son after being separated from her husband, who travelled for treatment during the genocide.
“Of course, there is no way to find a new toilet seat at an affordable price right now. The second-hand ones are also unsuitable and still expensive.”
Due to their scarcity, toilet seats in Gaza now cost between 1,500 and 2,000 shekels ($486-648).
“I have done everything possible to move from my tent so that we wouldn’t get soaked by rainwater like we did last year. But the garage I found doesn’t have a toilet, so we have to build our own,” Awad told Middle East Eye.
“I consider the garage rent affordable after all the other unaffordable apartments I tried to rent. It costs around 600 shekels ($194) a month. But now I have to find a toilet that costs twice as much as the rent.”

on

The Brighton conference revealed a party riding a wave of support but wrestling with internal tensions, political strategy and how to make an impact in Burnham's Britain
When I sat down with Mothin Ali early on Sunday, he was in an energetic mood.
It was the third and final day of what must have been an arduous Green Party conference for its co-deputy leader, who was dressed in his usual suit and flat cap.
"It's been a fantastic year," Ali beamed. "We had 400 councillors elected in May, 1,300 councillors in all, a fifth MP in parliament and our membership has quadrupled.
"It's a phenomenal record so far."
The Greens surged in the polls last year after Polanski was elected leader. They gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did.
Polanski is at least partially responsible for Keir Starmer's downfall and Andy Burnham's premiership. On Friday evening the renowned political analyst John Curtice argued as much at a packed fringe event.
The conference in the sunny seaside town of Brighton was full of energy. For many members it was the event of the year: friends roved the conference in groups and went off to restaurants and bars in the evening. They were diverse in age and ethnicity; many wore keffiyehs and Palestine badges.
But as Curtice pointed out - turning smiles into frowns - the Greens now have their work cut out for them under a new and much more popular prime minister.
Polling shows support for the Greens has plummeted in the past few months.
Andy Burnham has taken steps to address key grievances that led Labour voters to switch to the Greens under Starmer.
So far, the most significant has been the Labour government's sanctions on Israeli settlements.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake?
data.author: Yunus Turhan
data.summary:
Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake?
Submitted by
Yunus Turhan
on
Thu, 10/01/2026 - 16:33
When past leaders have tried to govern from a single centre, the country's peripheries have united in opposition
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed attends a meeting in Moscow on 25 September 2025 (Evgenia Novozhenina/AFP)
On
Ethiopia’s history has come back to haunt it.
Late last month, seven armed groups - among them the Fano militia in Amhara, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Oromo Liberation Army - announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, and vowed to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
Within days, Tigrayan forces had seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and opened fronts in Afar and Amhara. By 25 September, phone and internet lines in Tigray were cut. This time it was the TPLF, not Addis Ababa, that ordered the blackout.
Most commentary reads the new conflict as the collapse of the Pretoria agreement, a 2022 peace deal to end two years of war. But the story is much older than the Pretoria process and Abiy himself.
For nearly two centuries, Ethiopian politics has swung between a centre that wants to command, and regions that insist on ruling themselves. Each time the pendulum has pushed hard towards the centre, the peripheries have found a way to unite against it.
After the Zemane Mesafint (“Era of the Princes”) in the 18th and 19th centuries, when regional lords ran their own affairs, Tewodros II tried to rebuild the empire by the sword. The provinces revolted one after another, and in 1868, he died at Magdala, his army reduced to remnants.
Similarly, former emperor Haile Selassie’s 1962 dissolution of the Eritrean federation turned a small insurgency into a 30-year war. The Derg regime pushed centralisation to its limits, and fell in 1991 to a coalition of ethno-regional groups, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF).

data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Israel bans Zack Polanski after Green Party backs 'Zionism is racism' motion
Israel has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country after the party approved a motion at its conference declaring "Zionism is racism".
In a statement on Sunday, Israel accused the Green Party of England and Wales of legitimising "the destruction of the State of Israel".
Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the resolution, which also advocates for a one-state solution in historic Palestine, “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”.
“Therefore, as a first step, foreign minister Gideon Saar has decided this evening to declare Green Party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel,” it said.
According to Israel's Law of Return, persons with at least one Jewish grandparent, and their spouses, have a legal right to enter, reside in, and acquire citizenship of, the State of Israel.

data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
IRGC commander says US forces have ‘fled’ 1,000km from Iran’s borders
A top Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander said that the US army has moved 1,000km away from Iran's borders.
"The Americans fled and moved more than 1,000km away from our borders. This was not their choice; it was due to the authority of the Islamic Republic and the authority of the IRGC Ground Force," Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview.
He added that, for the first time, Washington's vessels were not present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or the northern Indian Ocean, saying that American warships are "100 percent vulnerable" to IRGC attacks.
Fadavi also stressed that the Strait of Hormuz remained under Tehran’s control, and said that the IRGC Navy warned ships using the US-supervised southern route in the waterway that "their vessels may be targeted at any point".
Only three to four million barrels of oil per day are now moving through the route, he claimed, dismissing the amount as "negligible" in contrast to pre-war traffic.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Can Baghdad gain control over paramilitary groups amid US war on Iran?
data.author: Zahra Ladha
data.summary:
Can Baghdad gain control over paramilitary groups amid US war on Iran?
Submitted by
Zahra Ladha
on
Fri, 10/02/2026 - 10:18
As the state seeks to bring armed groups under its control, competing interests and external pressures stand in the way
Popular Mobilisation Forces stand guard during a symbolic funeral procession celebrating the withdrawal of the US-led coalition from Iraq, in Baghdad on 1 October 2026 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP)
Off
With the US withdrawing its forces from its territories, Iraq is moving towards bringing the country’s powerful paramilitary groups under greater state control, a process that will require navigating competing interests among the groups, Baghdad and Washington.
It is unlikely to amount to straightforward disarmament, instead seeking to limit these groups’ ability to act autonomously by bringing their weapons more closely under state control and, in some cases, integrating fighters into formal state structures. Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has now set a deadline of 30 June 2027 to complete this process.
Whether the process succeeds will depend on Baghdad’s ability to manage the demands of armed groups, their willingness to accept limits on their autonomy and, crucially, whether external actors avoid actions that could undermine it.
In recent weeks, a framework for enforcing state control over Iraq’s paramilitary groups has emerged.
According to Zaidi, Baghdad plans to implement the process in phases, starting with a 90-day cessation of military activity. This period began on 30 September, on the same day the US-led coalition, which has for years come under attacks by these groups, officially withdrew from Iraq.
In return, the US would refrain from launching military strikes on armed groups in Iraq.

data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
US removes bombers from UK base at centre of mystery incident
The US has removed its B-1 bombers from a British air base one week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, a suspected plot that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham claimed was likely backed by Iran.
The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers 90 miles (145 km) west of London, which had recently been used for US strikes on Iran. A Pentagon official said on Sunday they had now returned to their home bases in the US.
Five men arrested by British police over the incident, which remains shrouded in mystery, have been released on bail. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, has also been released on bail.
Iran has said accusations it was involved in any plot are baseless, and its foreign minister, Abbas Aragchi, wrote on X: “I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree.”

New book by Andrew Feinstein traces $50bn in profit from the genocide in Gaza
BAE Systems' stand at the Defence and Security Equipment International fair at the ExCeL centre, in east London, on 9 September 2025 (AFP/Adrian Dennis)
Off
“The global trade in weapons is a business that counts its profits in billions, and its losses in human lives.”
This devastating balance sheet is the subject of Making a Killing: How the West Profits from Slaughter in Gaza and Yemen , a new book by arms corruption investigative organisation Shadow World Investigations, co-authored by Andrew Feinstein, Ruth Rohde and Jack Cinamon.
In it, they trace the rivers of blood that flow from the ruins of Gaza and Yemen into backroom meetings with politicians and arms manufacturing CEOs, exposing the corruption at the heart of the military-industrial complex – less a virus infecting the industry, but rather its lifeblood, keeping it alive.
The project began in 2017 with the intention of chronicling the Yemen crisis, but the authors incorporated Gaza after the start of the genocide in October 2023.
Due to be published in November, the work conveys the urgency and immediacy of conflicts coming to define the collapse of international order and the moral supremacy once claimed by western democracies.
Suffice to say, while the losses are never felt by the profiteers of war, the book delivers its own eulogy to some of its victims, through the voices of Palestinian journalist Ahmed Alnaouq, and the founders of Yemen-based Mwatana for Human Rights, Radhya al-Mutawakel and Abdulrasheed al-Faqih.
Mwatana is an organisation which aims to document civilian casualties from the war in Yemen not being recorded in international or regional media.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Three years after Israeli bombing, Palestinian man recovers wife's remains
data.author: Ahmed Dremly
data.summary:
Three years after Israeli bombing, Palestinian man recovers wife's remains
Submitted by
Ahmed Dremly
on
Mon, 10/05/2026 - 10:08
Adham Heriz spent years searching for his family beneath the ruins of their Gaza City home. A new civil defence operation recovered the remains of 105 Palestinians, but his son is still missing
A mass funeral for 105 Palestinians whose remains were recovered from beneath the rubble of destroyed buildings in the al-Taj area of Gaza City's al-Yarmouk neighbourhood, 1 October 2026 (Bilal Osama/Apaimages via Reuters)
Off
For nearly three years, Adham Heriz, 41, waited to recover and bury the bodies of his wife and children.
On Thursday, after years of searching through the ruins of their neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City, the Palestinian father finally recovered the remains of his wife, Hiam, 37. His son’s body is still missing.
Hiam and their eldest son, Anas, 17, were killed when a heavy Israeli bombardment completely destroyed their home in Al-Yarmouk on 25 October 2023.
According to the Palestinian civil defence spokesperson in Gaza, Mahmoud Basal, the attack involved a series of heavy Israeli bombardments that struck 18 buildings containing around 175 residential apartments.
Around 450 people were inside the buildings, including doctors, academics, journalists, children and infants, Basal told MEE.
“There were people thrown by the explosion around 200 metres. Entire families were wiped out. Many dead bodies were completely disintegrated, leaving little or no trace behind because of the massive explosives used in the bombs,” he said.
At the time, civil defence teams were able to recover only 120 bodies because Israeli forces were advancing and continuing to attack the area. Much of the heavy equipment and vehicles needed to move the rubble had also been destroyed.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Turkey supplies Korkut air defence systems to Ukraine, sources say
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Turkey supplies Korkut air defence systems to Ukraine, sources say
Turkey supplied anti-drone air defence systems to Ukraine earlier this year, allowing Kyiv to test new products and bolster its capabilities, several people familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye.
The sources said Ukraine had imported a small number of Turkish-made Korkut air defence systems, which typically consist of three weapon system vehicles and one command-and-control vehicle. They declined to disclose how many units had been deployed on the battlefield.
Produced by Aselsan, Korkut uses air defence guns to shoot down aerial targets, including the cruise missiles and drones that have become a persistent threat in the war in Ukraine. The system is designed to counter first-person-view and tethered drones using 25-millimetre smart ammunition.
“Korkut has been pretty much successful in countering the Russian attacks,” one Ukrainian official told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity due to government restrictions. “There were of course some problems but nothing that couldn’t be overcome through some small adjustments.”
The official said Korkut could be considered battle-proven and that Ukraine was interested in purchasing more systems.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Labour MP Emily Thornberry urges UK to defy Israeli order to close Jerusalem consulate
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Labour MP Emily Thornberry urges UK to defy Israeli order to close Jerusalem consulate
Emily Thornberry, chair of parliament’s influential Foreign Affairs Committee, has called on Britain to refuse compliance with Israel’s closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.
Her intervention comes amidst mounting anxiety among Palestinians that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will submit to Israeli pressure and shut the consulate on Thursday.
Middle East Eye understands that the foreign secretary’s decision is being watched closely by other consulates, including France and Spain, who fear they will be next to be forced out if the British quit.
Thornberry told MEE on Monday that the closure of the consulate was a “blatant retaliation against Britain for standing up for international law. The closure order is in itself illegal.”
“I hope that Israel will not go through with the closure of a consulate which has served Britons and Palestinians since 1838. Britain should not allow Israel to do this,” she said.

Investigation shows how the Foreign Office repeatedly failed to hold the Israeli army to account for war crimes
Pro-Palestinian activists and supporters gather in central London to protest British arms exports to Israel, on 17 April 2024 (Justin Tallis/AFP)
Off
Twenty-five years have passed since sociologist Stanley Cohen asked a question that remains just as urgent today as it was when he first posed it.
How is it that institutions, governments and ordinary people can know about atrocities, mass killing and human rights abuses, but simultaneously manage to put them out of their minds?
His brilliant study, States of Denial: Knowing About Atrocities and Suffering , drew on Cohen’s own reporting of cover-ups, disappearances and torture in his native South Africa. Yet its examination of the ways in which we pretend to ourselves that terrible events are not taking place was broader, taking in Latin America, the Rwanda genocide, the Holocaust, the Middle East and other examples.
Cohen distinguished between the different ways in which politicians, journalists and others have suppressed knowledge of the truth. He identified what he called “literal denial” - the unblinking assertion that crimes are not taking place.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent speech to the United Nations contained numerous examples of literal denial. He said that the ratio of civilian casualties to combatants in Gaza was exceptionally low, that Israel did not block aid to Gaza, and that Hamas should be blamed for shortages.
He also made the nonsensical assertion that settler violence in the occupied West Bank was down to a “handful of young juvenile delinquents”.
